author: charles-h-spurgeon
fields.title: All of Grace (For Teens)
fields.description: Charles Spurgeon wrote this short book for ordinary people who were sure God was only for the good — and told them plainly that salvation is “all of grace”: free, undeserved, for nothing. This teen retelling keeps his unforgettable pictures — the woman hiding from the rent man, the rope above Niagara, the limpet on the rock — and asks what grace actually changes in your life.

qa.question: Isn’t this just an old sermon telling me to try harder and be good?
qa.answer: It’s nearly the opposite. Spurgeon opens by saying he is “not calling for the rent”: the book doesn’t make demands, it brings a free gift. Its whole message is that God saves people who can’t save themselves.

qa.question: What does “justified” even mean?
qa.answer: It means being counted right — not guilty — before God. Spurgeon explains that God can do this justly because Jesus took the penalty in our place, and once the highest Judge has acquitted you, no one can condemn you.

qa.question: Why would God justify the ungodly instead of the good people?
qa.answer: Because, as the Bible says, there is “none righteous, no, not one.” A doctor is for the sick and pardon is for the guilty, so Spurgeon says being a sinner isn’t what keeps you out — it’s the very reason the good news is for you.

qa.question: Do I have to clean myself up before I come to God?
qa.answer: No. Spurgeon tells of a ragged street-sweeper who was sent away from an artist’s studio because he turned up washed and in a borrowed suit — he was wanted as he was. God’s grace meets you in your worst state.

qa.question: If it’s all grace, does it matter how I live?
qa.answer: Very much. Spurgeon insists that God gives a new heart along with forgiveness, that repentance and forgiveness always come together, and that faith which refuses to obey Jesus is only a pretence. Grace doesn’t leave you the same — it changes the direction of your life.

qa.question: What if I don’t feel anything?
qa.answer: Faith is trusting Christ, not having a certain feeling. Spurgeon admits he once wept because he couldn’t weep, and he compares mature faith to a sailor who steers by compass and stars without seeing land — trusting God’s word rather than his own feelings.

qa.question: What if I start following Jesus and then fall away?
qa.answer: Spurgeon says people turn back when they trust Jesus for the start and themselves for the finish. The answer is that “God is faithful”: he finishes what he begins, and since believers are joined to Christ, “unless Jesus sinks, the believer will never drown.”

fields.title: Not Calling for the Rent
fields.body_html:
“Come now, let us reason together, says the LORD: though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they are red like crimson, they shall become like wool.” — Isaiah 1:18 (ESV)

Spurgeon opens his book with a picture. A man once set up a drinking fountain by a busy roadside and hung a cup beside it on a little chain. Some time later he was told that a famous art critic had found a lot of fault with its design. The man only asked one thing: did many thirsty people drink at it? Thousands, they told him — poor men, women and children, every day. He smiled. He wasn’t bothered by the critic; he just hoped that on some hot summer’s day the critic himself might fill the cup and be refreshed. Then Spurgeon turns to you: “Here is my fountain, and here is my cup: find fault if you please; but do drink of the water of life.” He wrote in the plainest words he could on purpose, and he tells you straight what the book is for — nothing less than you finding Christ.

Then he tells a story he heard from the north of England. A minister knew a woman in his area was very poor, so one day he went to her house with money in his hand to help her. He knocked. Nothing. He knocked again, several times, and finally decided she must be out. A little later he met her at church and told her he’d called round about noon. “Oh, dear,” she said. “I heard you, sir, and I am so sorry I did not answer; but I thought it was the man calling for the rent.”

That, Spurgeon says, is exactly how most people hear anything about God. They hear the knock and assume someone has come to collect — duty, demands, a bill they know they can’t pay. So they stay quiet behind the door and pretend they’re not home. He wants to be heard, so he says it as plainly as he can: “I am not calling for the rent.” This book isn’t here to ask anything of you. It’s here to tell you that “salvation is all of grace, which means, free, gratis, for nothing.” It isn’t going to talk about law and punishment but about love, goodness, forgiveness, mercy and eternal life. And the one really knocking, he says, is Jesus, who “knocks with a hand which was nailed to the tree for such as you are.” God wouldn’t invite you to talk if he didn’t mean you well. So, Spurgeon says, “Open the door, and let my pleadings enter.”

Now — what is this actually about? You might be hiding from a gift because you think it’s a bill. A lot of people carry around a picture of God as a kind of landlord: someone who only turns up to tell you what you owe and where you’ve fallen short. So whenever anything about God comes near — a conversation, a verse, a thought at two in the morning — you go quiet behind the curtain and wait for it to leave. Spurgeon’s opening move is to say: you’ve misread the knock.

Notice why the woman hid. It wasn’t because she was wicked; it was because she was poor and knew she couldn’t pay. If that’s you — if you’ve kept God at arm’s length because you’re sure you could never measure up — then the knock is meant for exactly you. Spurgeon isn’t pretending it doesn’t matter how you live; the book will get there. He’s saying the first word from God is not a demand. It’s an offer. He even points out that reading is a kind of hearing, and “faith may come to you while you are reading this book.” So don’t read the next chapters with your shoulders braced for a lecture.

One thing to do this week: catch your reflex. Each time God, church or the Bible comes up this week, notice what you instantly expect — a rule, a guilt trip, a demand? Then write one honest sentence: “I think what God wants from me is ___.” Keep it, and read it again when you finish this book. Ask yourself whether the door you’ve kept shut was ever really the rent man.

study_questions.question: Why didn’t the poor woman open the door when the minister knocked?
study_questions.answer: She heard him but thought it was the man calling for the rent, so she pretended not to be home — even though he had come to give her money.

study_questions.question: What does Spurgeon mean when he says “I am not calling for the rent”?
study_questions.answer: He means the book isn’t making a demand on the reader but bringing a free gift: salvation that is “all of grace” — free, for nothing.

study_questions.question: What do you usually expect God to want from you? How might it change things if the first word is an offer, not a bill?
study_questions.answer: The chapter’s point: many people hide from God because they think he has come to collect what they can’t pay. If the knock is a gift, the thing to do is stop hiding and open the door.

fields.title: Good News for the Ungodly
fields.body_html:
“And to the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness.” — Romans 4:5 (ESV)

Spurgeon builds this chapter on four words from Romans: God “justifies the ungodly.” He admits they shocked him and kept on shocking him. People who hated the Christian message used to throw it at God as an accusation — he takes in the worst people! — and Spurgeon points out that the Bible doesn’t deny it. It owns it. God gives himself the title. Most of us assume salvation is for good people, and that if we were better God would reward us. But God, who sees through everything, knows there is “none righteous, no, not one.” So Jesus didn’t come looking for goodness to reward. “He comes, not because we are just, but to make us so.”

Think about how strange that is. A good lawyer defends innocent people; he isn’t supposed to get the guilty off. Making a guilty person truly right before a court is beyond any human. “To justify the ungodly — this is a miracle worthy of a God.” And Spurgeon says it has to be this way. A doctor with a sure cure isn’t sent to a town where nobody is sick. A generous man who decides to cancel debts can only cancel them for people who actually owe him. Forgiveness is only for the guilty. So if you think you must be lost because you are a sinner, he turns it around: that’s the very reason you can be saved. “The sinner is the gospel’s reason for existence.”

He describes two kinds of ungodly people. One has lived as if there were no God at all. The other has gone to every service, maybe even sung in the choir, and never once met God for himself. Both, he says, are exactly who this message is for. The only people it can’t help are those who think they don’t need it — whose own goodness, he warns, is “not half so substantial as a cobweb.” Then a story. An artist painting a scene of his city wanted a well-known ragged street-sweeper in the picture and offered to pay him to come to the studio. The man arrived next morning washed, combed and in a borrowed suit — and was sent away. He was wanted as he was. “Wait not for reformation, but come at once for salvation.”

He adds one more story. A preacher once gave such a fierce sermon on judgment that a listener told him it belonged in the county jail, preached to criminals. “Oh, no,” the preacher said — in the jail he would have preached a different text: “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners.” Spurgeon’s comment sums up the whole chapter: “The law is for the self-righteous, to humble their pride: the gospel is for the lost, to remove their despair.”

Now — what is this actually about? God’s grace starts where you actually are, not where you think you should be. Most of us have a quiet rule running in the background: get yourself sorted, then approach God. Stop the thing you’re ashamed of, get your head straight, become the kind of person who belongs — and then maybe. Spurgeon says that rule is upside down. The gospel isn’t a prize for people who’ve cleaned up. It’s a rescue for people who can’t.

That’s hard on your pride and wonderful for your despair. Hard on your pride because being “a good kid” or “a decent person” doesn’t earn you anything here. Wonderful for your despair because the worst thing you know about yourself doesn’t disqualify you; it’s the very category God says he works with. God forgives, Spurgeon says, “not because they are good, but because He is good.”

One thing to do this week: notice the moment you want to “wash your face” before you pray — to wait until you feel less guilty, less messy, more spiritual. Don’t wait. Pray once this week exactly as you are, in plain words, with nothing touched up: “God, I’m ungodly. You say you justify the ungodly. I’m asking you to do that for me.”

study_questions.question: Why was the street-sweeper sent away from the artist’s studio?
study_questions.answer: He had washed, combed his hair and put on a respectable suit, but the artist wanted to paint him as the ragged sweeper everyone knew. He was needed as he was.

study_questions.question: Why does Spurgeon say forgiveness can only be for the guilty?
study_questions.answer: A doctor is for the sick and a debt can only be cancelled for someone who owes it. In the same way, God’s pardon is only for those who have actually sinned — so being a sinner is the reason you can be saved, not the reason you can’t.

study_questions.question: Is there something you feel you need to fix before God would want you? What does this chapter say to that?
study_questions.answer: The chapter’s point: God justifies the ungodly, and his grace meets you in your worst state. Waiting to clean yourself up first is the street-sweeper’s mistake — come as you are.

fields.title: How a Just God Can Forgive
fields.body_html:
“It was to show his righteousness at the present time, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus.” — Romans 3:26 (ESV)

To be “justified” means to be counted right — not guilty — before God. Spurgeon points out that you can’t do it for yourself (you’d just be fooling yourself), and other people can’t do it for you either: some will praise you for small favours and others will run you down for less. Only one opinion counts. “It is God that justifieth.” And only God can, because your sin is against him. If someone hurts you, only you can forgive them; a stranger can’t do it on your behalf. That’s why no priest or go-between can stand in for you, he says — “you had better see to your soul’s matters yourself.” Look at Saul, who hunted Christians like a wolf among sheep, and became the greatest preacher of this very message. Or think of the prodigal son in Jesus’ story: his father ran to welcome him home with as much love as if he had never left — so much that the older brother grumbled. Spurgeon applies it straight to you: if you come back to God, “He will treat you as if you had never done wrong!”

And when God does it, it is settled. “If the Judge acquits me, who can condemn me?” Spurgeon tells his own story here. As a teenager he was crushed by guilt; life was a misery. Then he heard the words, “Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth.” “I looked, and in a moment the Lord justified me.” He says he became as sure he was forgiven as he had been sure he was condemned — on the same evidence, God’s word.

But that raised a hard question, one he couldn’t shake. In those dark months he had actually felt that God ought to punish him. Forgiveness that just shrugged at sin wouldn’t have satisfied his conscience. So how can God be just and still let the guilty go? The answer, he says, is something no one could have invented: the Judge’s own Son took the sentence. Jesus “bore my sin in His own body on the tree.” God didn’t lower the standard or blunt the sword; the penalty was really paid, by someone who could pay it. “God will spare the sinner because He did not spare His Son.” And if Jesus died in your place, why should you die too?

Then the picture: a shipwreck, and a lifeboat alongside. “I have nothing with me,” you say. Nobody asked you to bring anything. People escaping for their lives leave even their clothes behind. “Leap for it, just as you are.” And Spurgeon puts himself in the boat beside you: his only hope is the cross, and “if you perish trusting Him, I must perish too.”

Now — what is this actually about? Real forgiveness doesn’t pretend sin didn’t matter; it means someone paid for it. You probably know the difference. When someone says “it’s fine, whatever” about something that clearly wasn’t fine, it doesn’t actually feel like forgiveness — it feels like they didn’t take you seriously. Deep down we know wrong has a cost. Spurgeon’s whole point is that at the cross God takes your wrong completely seriously and lets you go free, because Jesus carried the cost himself.

That’s why being justified by God is more solid than any amount of being liked, being told you’re a good person, or trying to feel okay about yourself. Those verdicts change with the weather. God’s doesn’t — it rests on something already done. Spurgeon even says a forgiven sinner stands on surer ground than someone trying to be good enough, because the one trying could never be sure he had done enough. Grace isn’t only kinder than effort; it is more certain.

One thing to do this week: read one of the accounts of Jesus’ death slowly — Luke 23 is a good one. When you reach the cross, stop and say to yourself, honestly and personally: “That was the cost of what I’ve done, and he paid it.” Then do what Spurgeon did. Don’t analyse it to death. Look.

study_questions.question: What words was Spurgeon given when he was crushed by guilt, and what happened?
study_questions.answer: He heard “Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth.” He looked to Christ, and says that in a moment the Lord justified him and gave him peace.

study_questions.question: How can God be both completely just and still forgive the guilty?
study_questions.answer: Because Jesus, God’s own Son, took the punishment in our place. The penalty was really paid, so God can forgive without pretending sin doesn’t matter.

study_questions.question: Whose verdict on you do you lean on most — friends, family, your own feelings? How is God’s verdict different?
study_questions.answer: The chapter’s point: other people’s opinions shift, and justifying yourself is self-deception. When God justifies someone because of Christ’s sacrifice, it is settled — “If the Judge acquits me, who can condemn me?”

fields.title: A New Heart
fields.body_html:
“And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you. And I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh.” — Ezekiel 36:26 (ESV)

Some people get the idea of being forgiven, Spurgeon says, and their problem is something else: they can’t stop sinning. They try to tame their own nature and it won’t be tamed. Their thoughts run off, their desires are wild, their temper flares, and they feel as if they have “a den of wild beasts” inside. Like a stone thrown in the air, they get lifted up by a good sermon and then drop straight back down. If that’s you, he says, then good — because salvation that didn’t deal with this wouldn’t be salvation at all. “We want to be purified as well as pardoned.” Forgiveness without change would be like declaring a leper clean and leaving him to die of the disease.

Jesus came to deal with sin three ways, he explains: its penalty, its power, and, one day, its presence. The penalty is dealt with at the cross. The power can be broken now. And for that, God makes a promise in Ezekiel — notice it’s all “I will”: I will give you a new heart, I will take away the heart of stone. You can’t change your own heart. God knows that. He also knows he can. Spurgeon compares it to standing at the bottom of Niagara Falls and speaking a word that makes the whole river run back up the cliff. That’s the size of the change when God reverses the direction of a human life.

Then a homely picture he borrowed from another preacher. Watch a cat: she washes herself carefully with her paws and tongue. Have you ever seen a pig do that? You can scrub a pig, but it will run straight back to the mud — it’s against its nature to stay clean. “The only way in which you can get a sow to wash itself is to transform it into a cat.” Same with us. You can teach someone good habits and set a good example, but until they get a new nature, holiness feels like swimming upstream. Once God changes the heart, it starts to go the other way naturally. One convert told Spurgeon, “Either all the world is changed, or else I am.” He’d seen it himself — thieves made honest, drunkards sober, liars truthful.

He describes the change in pictures: “The lion of anger shall give place to the lamb of meekness.” Where everything was hard, things become tender. “I cannot make this change,” someone says. Spurgeon’s answer: “Who said you could?” The promise isn’t about what you will do. It’s about what God will do. And if you ask exactly how God will do it, he is blunt again: “What business is that of yours?” The one who made the promise is responsible for keeping it.

Now — what is this actually about? Christianity isn’t a self-improvement plan; it’s God giving you a new heart. Most of us approach our worst habits with willpower: a new rule, a promise, an app, a fresh start on Monday. Sometimes that helps for a while. But Spurgeon is honest that you can’t white-knuckle your way into a different nature. The pig can be hosed down; it’s still a pig.

That isn’t an excuse to give up the fight. It’s a change in where your hope sits. Instead of “I have to become someone else before God will accept me,” it’s “God accepts me in Christ and has promised to make me someone new.” The change may feel slow. fields.title: Grace Is the Fountain
fields.body_html:
“For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God.” — Ephesians 2:8 (ESV)

Before explaining faith, Spurgeon wants you to stand at the source. “By grace are ye saved.” People are forgiven and changed not because of anything in them but because God is gracious — full of love, pity and mercy that never runs out. Faith matters, but it isn’t the spring the water comes from. Faith is the pipe. He thinks of the great old aqueducts around Rome, broken arches that no longer carry water to the city. Faith is the aqueduct that brings the water down to thirsty people — but it is not the water. So he warns: “Never make a Christ out of your faith.” The power isn’t in your believing; it’s in the God you believe in.

That’s good news if your faith feels weak. “A trembling hand may receive a golden gift.” A thin wire can carry an important message. So, he says, “Think more of Him to whom you look than of the look itself.”

Then he tries to say what faith actually is, while admitting that most definitions made him understand it less. Faith, he says, has three parts. First, knowledge: you can’t trust someone you’ve never heard of, so find out who Jesus is and what he did — especially that he died in the place of sinners. Second, belief: being convinced it’s actually true, the way you believe your father or a friend you trust. Third, and essential, trust. The old Puritans had a word for faith: “recumbency” — leaning on something. “Lean with all your weight upon Christ.” Better still, he says, “fall at full length, and lie on the Rock of Ages.”

Put another way: faith believes Jesus is who he says he is, believes he will do what he promised — he said he’d turn away no one who comes — and then expects it of him. And Spurgeon’s fear is that you’ll understand all this and never do it. A hungry man doesn’t need to understand digestion to eat; he eats and lives. A food scientist who never eats will starve with all his knowledge. “Better the poorest real faith actually at work, than the best ideal of it left in the region of speculation.” He is sobering about it: plenty of people have understood the doctrine of faith perfectly and never trusted. But not one person who has trusted Jesus has ever been turned away — even if they could never have explained their faith in words.

Notice, too, what faith is not. It isn’t blind, because it starts with knowing something. It isn’t a guess, because it believes facts it is sure of. And it isn’t a daydream, because it stakes everything on what God has said.

Now — what is this actually about? Faith isn’t a feeling or a performance; it’s putting your full weight on Jesus. A lot of people think faith means feeling very sure, or very spiritual, or having no doubts. So they spend their energy staring at their own faith, checking whether it’s strong enough. Spurgeon says that’s like staring at the pipe and wondering why you’re still thirsty. Look at the fountain.

Think of sitting down on a chair. You don’t need to feel confident about chairs; you just sit, and the chair holds you. The holding is the chair’s job. Faith is the sitting down. It can be shaky and still be real, because what saves you is not how hard you lean but who you’re leaning on. Some days you’ll feel certain and some days you won’t. The chair doesn’t change either way, and neither does Jesus.

One thing to do this week: do the three parts on purpose. Know: read John 3:14–18 and write down what Jesus says about himself. Believe: ask yourself honestly, “Do I think this is true?” Trust: if the answer is yes, tell him in your own words that you are leaning your whole weight on him — not on how you feel about it.

study_questions.question: Do you tend to check how strong your faith feels? What would it mean to look at Jesus instead?

fields.title: Pictures of Faith
fields.body_html:
“For we walk by faith, not by sight.” — 2 Corinthians 5:7 (ESV)

Because faith is simple but hard to explain, Spurgeon gives a whole run of pictures. Faith is like the eye: with one glance you can take in the sun and the far-off stars, and in the same way trust brings Jesus near, though he is in heaven. Faith is like the hand: it takes hold and says, “This is mine.” You won’t be stealing; you have permission — “whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely.” And faith is like the mouth: food only does you good once you take it in, and a hungry person doesn’t need lessons in eating.

Then everyday life. A farmer buries seed and expects a harvest. A businessman hands his money to a bank and sleeps better than if it were locked in his own safe. A goldsmith puts precious metal into a fire that looks as if it will destroy it, and gets it back purer. You can’t turn anywhere, Spurgeon says, without seeing people trust. A swimmer has to lift his feet off the bottom and let the water hold him; he can’t swim otherwise. And then the limpet — a little shellfish stuck on a rock by the sea. Tap the first one sharply and you can knock it off. But the next one has heard the blow, and now it clings with everything it has; you’ll break the rock before you move it. It knows nothing about geology. It just clings. “It is the limpet’s life to cling to the rock, and it is the sinner’s life to cling to Jesus.” Thousands of Christians, he says, have no more faith than that — and it is enough.

Faith can grow into something more. A blind man takes the arm of a friend who can see, because he knows his friend has what he lacks. A student believes his teacher about countries he has never visited. Deeper still is faith that grows from love: Spurgeon pictures the wife of a brilliant doctor who falls dangerously ill but stays calm, because her husband has healed thousands with her disease and she knows he loves her. And faith obeys — a ship’s captain who trusts the pilot steers where the pilot says. “Faith which refuses to obey the commands of the Saviour is a mere pretence.”

Last, mature faith. One old Christian wrote “T” and “P” in the margin of her Bible beside every promise she had tried and proved. And Spurgeon marvels at a ship’s captain who sails for weeks without seeing land, steering by compass and stars, and arrives exactly at the harbour. That, he says, is what it is to say goodbye to the shores of “sight and feeling” and steer by God’s word.

Now — what is this actually about? Real faith can be small and simple and still hold on to Jesus. You might think you need to understand everything, answer every objection, or feel deeply before your faith counts. The limpet understands nothing and clings, and it is safe. Faith grows — from clinging, to trusting a guide, to love, to the kind that has tested God’s promises for years — but it starts small, and small is real.

Notice, though, that every picture has something in common: the person stops relying on themselves. The swimmer lifts his feet. The blind man takes an arm. The patient follows the doctor. Faith isn’t only an opinion in your head; it shows up in what you lean on and whose directions you follow. You already trust all day long — the bus driver, the doctor, the friend who says they’ll be there. The question isn’t whether you can trust. It’s whether you will trust Jesus the way you trust them.

One thing to do this week: start your own “T and P.” Pick one promise — for example, Jesus’ words in John 6:37, “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” — and write it somewhere you’ll see it. Act on it this week. Then, when you’ve seen it hold, write the letters next to it. That’s how faith that clings becomes faith that knows.

study_questions.question: What does the limpet do when it hears the blow on its neighbour, and what does Spurgeon compare it to?
study_questions.answer: It clings to the rock with all its might so it can’t be knocked off. He says it is the limpet’s life to cling to the rock, and the sinner’s life to cling to Jesus.

study_questions.question: Why does Spurgeon include obedience among his pictures of faith?
study_questions.answer: Because trust shows itself in action: a captain who trusts the pilot follows his directions. Faith that refuses to do what Jesus says is only pretending.

study_questions.question: Which picture of faith fits you best right now — the limpet, the blind man, the doctor’s wife, the sailor? Why?
study_questions.answer: The chapter’s point: faith comes in different sizes and grows over time, but even the smallest real clinging to Jesus is enough to be safe. Start where you are and let it grow.

fields.title: Why Faith? The Rope and the Log
fields.body_html:
“For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9 (ESV)

Why did God choose faith, and not love or patience or good behaviour, as the way we receive salvation? Spurgeon is careful — God doesn’t owe us explanations — but he offers some reasons. The first is simple: faith is made for receiving. If you give a poor man a coin, you put it in his hand, not his ear or on his foot. Or picture holding out an apple to a small child. “The child’s hand does not make the apple, nor improve the apple, nor deserve the apple; it only takes it.” Faith is like that. He quotes an old saying: faith is “the tongue that begs pardon, the hand which receives it, and the eye which sees it; but it is not the price which buys it.”

Second, faith gives all the credit to God. God can’t stand pride, and he won’t save people in a way that lets them strut. A hand that takes a gift doesn’t expect to be thanked for taking it. So faith, Spurgeon says, “sets the crown upon the right head.”

Third, faith actually connects you to God. Here is the picture he says he couldn’t improve on. Years ago a boat overturned above Niagara Falls and two men were swept toward the edge. People on the bank floated a rope out, and both men grabbed it. One held on and was pulled to safety. The other saw a huge log floating past and let go of the rope to grab the log, because it was bigger and looked safer. The log went over the falls with him on it. It was big, but it wasn’t attached to the shore. That, says Spurgeon, is what trusting your own works or religious rituals is like — impressive, but not connected to anything. Faith can look like a thin cord, but the other end is in God’s hands, and he is the one pulling.

Fourth, faith is the mainspring of everything we do. Spurgeon notes that he only walks across his study because he believes his legs will carry him; people go to work because they believe in wages. So when God creates faith in us, he takes hold of the very thing that moves us — and from there love, prayer, holiness and courage follow. He quotes an old line: “What oil is to the wheels, what weights are to a clock, what wings are to a bird, what sails are to a ship, that faith is to all holy duties and services.” Faith also works through love, and it brings peace and joy. And he finishes with an old preacher’s picture. One servant throws his shoulder at a locked door and pushes with all his strength, and it doesn’t move. Another comes with the key and walks straight in. Trying to be saved by works is pushing at heaven’s gate. Faith, the old preacher said, “is the key which opens the gate at once.”

Now — what is this actually about? Faith saves not because it’s impressive but because it connects you to the One who is. The log is everything we’re tempted to cling to because it feels bigger: being a good person, doing more than others, going to church, keeping the rules, being right. Those things aren’t worthless, but they aren’t tied to the shore. What gets you out of the current is being joined to Jesus.

This also kills two opposite problems. If you’ve been proud of your own goodness, faith gives you nothing to boast about — you only took what was handed to you. If you’ve felt you have nothing to offer, faith doesn’t ask you to offer anything. An empty hand is exactly the right shape.

One thing to do this week: make two lists. On one side, write the “logs” you tend to rely on to feel okay before God — your grades, your reputation, your church attendance, your niceness. On the other, write one sentence about the rope: what Jesus has done for you. Then pray, specifically, letting go of the first list and holding on to the second.

study_questions.question: What happened to the two men swept toward Niagara Falls?
study_questions.answer: Both grabbed the rope thrown from the shore. One held on and was pulled to safety; the other let go to grab a big log, which went over the falls with him because it wasn’t connected to the shore.

study_questions.answer: Like a child’s hand taking an apple, faith doesn’t make, improve or deserve the gift — it only takes it. So it gives all the glory to God and leaves no room for boasting.

study_questions.answer: The chapter’s point: our own works and religious habits may look bigger and safer, but they aren’t connected to the shore. Only faith joins you to Christ, who does the pulling.

fields.title: “I Can’t Do Anything”
fields.body_html:
“For while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly.” — Romans 5:6 (ESV)

Some people believe everything so far and still groan, “I can do nothing.” It isn’t an excuse; they would if they could. Spurgeon compares it to a doctor telling a starving widow her sick son needs fine wine and a holiday at a spa — good advice, impossible to follow. But the gospel, he says, “begins where we are.” When the Good Samaritan found the beaten traveller, he didn’t tell him to get up and walk to the inn. He “came where he was” and carried him. And Spurgeon holds one verse up against every kind of helplessness: when we were “without strength,” Christ died for the ungodly. Not when we were a bit weak — when we had no strength at all.

Then he goes through the excuses one by one. I can’t think deeply enough. You don’t need to. Salvation needs “a simple reliance upon Jesus,” not long reasoning. Let that one verse sit on your tongue like a sweet. I can’t repent enough. Spurgeon admits he went through exactly this: “I used to get into a corner and weep, because I could not weep.” His heart broke because he thought it wouldn’t break. Repenting, he explains, is turning your mind from sin to Christ, and no one is ever satisfied with their own repentance. And you don’t get there by squeezing out feelings: “Repentance will not make you see Christ; but to see Christ will give you repentance.”

fields.title: How Faith Grows
fields.body_html:
“So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ.” — Romans 10:17 (ESV)

“How do I get more faith?” Spurgeon says a lot of nonsense gets talked about this, so he gets practical. The first answer is almost blunt: “The shortest way to believe is to believe.” But if you’re stuck, take it to God — tell him exactly what puzzles you, the way you’d ask an author what he meant. Hear the gospel often; we come to believe things we hear again and again. Listen to people who’ve been changed; you’ll find someone just like you. He tells of a man from a hot country who refused to believe water could turn hard enough to walk on. When he finally saw a frozen river, he still wouldn’t step onto it — until he watched others walk across safely. Then he trusted it too.

Even better, look at who is telling you to believe. A factory foreman was afraid he had no right to come to Christ. His employer sent a card round: “Come to my house immediately after work.” When John turned up, the boss pretended to be annoyed — what right did he have to call at this hour? “As you sent for me,” John said, “I had a right to come.” Then the boss read him Jesus’ words: “Come unto me, all ye that labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” John saw it at once. If Jesus has invited you, you can’t be wrong to come. And if you still can’t trust him, ask why. He’s never done anything to deserve your distrust. “They made Him a martyr; but you make Him a liar.” So Spurgeon flips the question: “Do not ask how can I believe? But answer another question — How can you disbelieve?” Sometimes, he says, the real block is pride — a quarrel with God you haven’t dropped, a wish to keep your own way. His advice is to surrender, and he says he believes no one ever threw up their hands and cried, “Lord, I yield,” without finding before long that faith had become easy.

Then someone objects: Jesus said, “You must be born again,” and that’s something only God can do. True, says Spurgeon — but the same chapter in John says that whoever believes in him will not perish. Both came from the same lips. “It is ours to believe, it is the Lord’s to create us anew.” The Spirit’s work is like the wind, Jesus said: you can’t see where it comes from, only what it does. A farmer can’t make seed grow either, but that’s no excuse not to sow. And your believing is itself the evidence that the Spirit is already at work.

Finally, remember that you’re not trusting a dead hero. Jesus rose and is alive, interceding for sinners at God’s right hand, with all authority in heaven and earth. “We have a Friend at court; yea, a Friend on the throne.” Put your case in his hands: “No suit ever failed which was left with this great Advocate.”

Now — what is this actually about? Faith grows by looking at Jesus, not by looking at your faith. When people want “more faith,” they usually try to manufacture a feeling. Spurgeon’s advice is the opposite: get closer to the evidence. Hear the message more. Hang around people it has changed. Notice that Jesus actually invited you. Think about who he is. Faith is a response to something outside you; feed it with that.

And don’t let the deep questions — How does the new birth work? How does God’s part fit with mine? — become a reason to stay on the shore. Nobody refuses a lifeboat because they don’t understand buoyancy.

One thing to do this week: ask one Christian you respect to tell you, in ten minutes, how they came to trust Jesus — and what they were like before. Then read Matthew 11:28 and treat it as John treated his boss’s card: an invitation with your name on it.

study_questions.question: Why did the foreman John feel he had the right to go to his employer’s house after work?
study_questions.answer: Because his employer had sent him a card telling him to come. His boss then showed him that Jesus’ invitation, “Come unto me,” gave him the same right to come to Christ.

study_questions.question: How does Spurgeon fit together “You must be born again” and “whoever believes will not perish”?
study_questions.answer: Both are true and come from Jesus. It is our part to believe and God’s part to make us new; God gives the new birth to all who believe, and believing is the evidence the Spirit is already at work.

study_questions.question: What is one thing you could do this week to “hear” more — and whose story could you listen to?
study_questions.answer: The chapter’s point: faith comes by hearing, by others’ testimony, and above all by seeing who invites you. The shortest way to believe is to believe — and a living Saviour is there to receive you.

fields.title: Turning Around
fields.body_html:
“God exalted him at his right hand as Leader and Savior, to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins.” — Acts 5:31 (ESV)

Spurgeon notices that in this verse repentance and forgiveness come from the same hand — the hand once nailed to the cross, now raised in glory. And they always go together. Forgiving someone who loves his sin and has no intention of leaving it would be a licence to keep doing wrong. It would also be a lame, half-finished mercy. What good is it, he asks, to be washed and then left lying in the mud? To bring a man out of the grave and leave him dead? Anyone whose heart has really been woken up doesn’t just want to escape punishment. They want to be free of sin itself.

So the two arrive together and stay together. Forgiveness leads to repentance — knowing you’re loved and pardoned is what makes you hate the thing that hurt Jesus. And repentance is a sign of forgiveness. “Faith and repentance are but two spokes in the same wheel, two handles of the same plough.” Repentance isn’t a few miserable days of penance to get over with; it’s “the grace of a lifetime.” He describes it as “a heart broken for sin, and from sin” — sorry about the past and set on a different future. But keep things in their places: “Do not regard your repentance as the cause of your remission, but as the companion of it.” You aren’t forgiven because you’re sorry enough.

Then how do you get repentance? From the same place as forgiveness. “Our Lord Jesus Christ has gone up that grace may come down.” He sends his Spirit to soften hard hearts. Without Jesus, Spurgeon says, being sorry would be worth nothing before God; the law just says the soul that sins will die. “We might feel remorse with its horrors, but never repentance with its hopes.” Jesus’ death and rising are what make turning back to God possible at all. Now he uses everything that happens to you — a rooster crowing, as it did for Peter, or an earthquake shaking a prison, as it did for the jailer at Philippi. “The Lord’s mercy often rides to the door of our hearts on the black horse of affliction.” And notice who Peter says Jesus gives repentance to: the very people who had shouted for his death. Nobody is too hard for him. Spurgeon quotes a hymn written by William Hone, a well-known sceptic who was won over: “The proudest heart that ever beat / Hath been subdued in me.”

So, he says, stop sitting in your room trying to squeeze out tears. “Do not sit down and try to pump up repentance from the dry well of corrupt nature.” Go and look at Jesus on the cross, and let him look at you, as he looked at Peter. “Look not beneath the ice to find fire.”

Now — what is this actually about? Repentance isn’t earning forgiveness; it’s turning around because you’ve been loved. Some people think repenting means feeling terrible for long enough that God is satisfied. Others think forgiveness means they never have to change. Spurgeon rejects both. Turning from sin isn’t the price of grace — but there’s no such thing as grace that leaves you facing the same way.

Real repentance often looks less dramatic than people expect. It looks like admitting you were wrong without excuses. It looks like deleting something, ending something, apologising to someone, and doing it again tomorrow when you slip. And the more sure you are of being forgiven, the more you’ll want to turn. If you’ve been waiting to feel crushed enough before you come to God, stop waiting: come and be forgiven, and the turning will grow out of that.

One thing to do this week: spend fifteen minutes with Luke 22:54–62, the night Peter denied Jesus and “the Lord turned and looked at Peter.” Then ask God to show you one thing you need to turn from — and take one concrete step away from it before the week is out. Don’t wait to feel sorry enough first.

study_questions.question: Why does Spurgeon say forgiveness without repentance would be a “lame” mercy?
study_questions.answer: Because it would leave the person in love with sin — like washing someone and leaving them in the mud. Real mercy frees us from sin’s power, not just its punishment.

study_questions.question: What does Spurgeon mean by “look not beneath the ice to find fire”?
study_questions.answer: He means you won’t find repentance by digging into your own cold heart. It comes as a gift from Jesus, especially as you look at his death for you.

study_questions.question: Is there something you’ve been waiting to feel sorry enough about before you turn from it? What would one concrete step look like?
study_questions.answer: The chapter’s point: repentance is the companion of forgiveness, not its cause, and Jesus gives both. Look to him, and turn — you don’t have to manufacture the tears first.

fields.title: Will I Fall Away?
fields.body_html:
“God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.” — 1 Corinthians 1:9 (ESV)

Many people coming to Christ are haunted by a fear: what if I start and then drift off? They’ve had good feelings before, they say, and those feelings vanished like early-morning dew. Spurgeon takes the fear seriously — and then points out the trap inside it. Some people really have turned back, he says, because they trusted Jesus to start them and trusted themselves to keep them going. “If we trust to ourselves for our holding on we shall not hold on.” A chain is only as strong as its weakest link; if Jesus is your hope for everything except one thing, that one thing will break. “If you look to Christ for your beginnings, beware of looking to yourself for your endings.”

And he doesn’t pretend holding on is easy. A marble statue needs no food, but a living person gets hungry every day; a living faith needs fresh grace every day. Some people are naturally restless, flitting like butterflies from one thing to another. All of us, he says, have shown enough foolishness “before the breakfast things are cleared away from the table” to make us ashamed. Life is long and tiring. Spurgeon borrows Bunyan’s map: the Christian road has its Hill of Difficulty and Valley of Humiliation, its Vanity Fair and its Castles of Despair as well as its Delectable Mountains. The world can be hostile. But think of it this way: God never provides anything we won’t need, so the very fact that he promises to keep us tells us we will need keeping. Real Christianity is “supernatural at its beginning, supernatural in its continuance, and supernatural in its close.”

So Paul’s promise matters: Jesus “will sustain you to the end, guiltless.” God strengthens what he starts. A young tree is helped to root itself “both by the soft showers and the rough winds” — the good days and the hard ones. And God doesn’t only want to keep you safe; he wants to keep you holy. “To be kept holy is better than merely to be kept safe.” Spurgeon is sad about Christians whose lives are a string of stumbles — “never quite down, and yet they are seldom on their feet.” That isn’t the plan. Jesus said, “I give unto my sheep eternal life; and they shall never perish.”

And why is Paul so sure? Not because the Corinthians were faithful. “God is faithful.” We are “variable as the wind, frail as a spider’s web, weak as water,” but God never starts a job and leaves it half done. “The saints shall persevere in holiness, because God perseveres in grace.” He has called you into partnership with his Son. Picture a business with two partners — one completely broke, the other unimaginably rich. Or, in Spurgeon’s plainest words: “Christ and the believing sinner are in the same boat: unless Jesus sinks, the believer will never drown.”

Now — what is this actually about? You don’t keep yourself saved; God keeps you, and that’s why you keep going. The fear of falling away is often a fear about yourself: I know how inconsistent I am. Spurgeon agrees you’re inconsistent. That’s exactly why your hope can’t rest on you. It rests on a faithful God who finishes what he starts.

But notice he never says, “So it doesn’t matter how you live.” Being kept by God looks like actually being kept — growing steadier, rooting deeper, getting back up. The security is the soil; holiness is the growth. And Spurgeon has a word for beginners who look at older, steadier Christians and think they’ll never be like that: you who are now a “babe” in Christ can one day be a “father” in the church — hoped for as a gift of grace, not earned by effort.

One thing to do this week: write down the thing you’re most afraid will pull you away from God — a friendship, a doubt, a habit, the fact that your feelings fade. Underneath it, write: “God is faithful” (1 Corinthians 1:9). Pray about that fear by name each night this week, and ask him for today’s grace, not next year’s.

study_questions.question: What mistake does Spurgeon say has caused some people to turn back?
study_questions.answer: They trusted Jesus for the beginning of their salvation but trusted themselves to keep going. If we trust ourselves for holding on, we won’t hold on.

study_questions.question: Why does Paul expect believers to be kept to the end, according to Spurgeon?
study_questions.answer: Not because they are faithful, but because “God is faithful.” He has called them into partnership with his Son, and he finishes what he starts — so unless Jesus sinks, the believer won’t drown.

study_questions.question: What are you most afraid might pull you away from God? How does God’s faithfulness speak to that fear?
study_questions.answer: The chapter’s point: the saints persevere because God perseveres in grace. Look to Christ for your ending as well as your beginning, and ask him daily for the grace to hold on.

One thing to do this week: write down the thing you’re most afraid will pull you away from God — a friendship, a doubt, a habit, the fact that your feelings fade. Underneath it, write: “God is faithful” (1 Corinthians 1:9). Pray about that fear by name each night this week, and ask him for today’s grace, not next year’s.

fields.title: Now
fields.body_html:
“Behold, now is the favorable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.” — 2 Corinthians 6:2 (ESV)

Spurgeon ends his book the way he started it — talking straight to you. Reading a book like this is pointless, he says, unless you actually take hold of what it says. “It is as if one saw plenty of food in a shop and yet remained hungry, for want of personally eating some.” He tells you he stopped writing at this very page, put down his pen and knelt to pray for whoever would read it. Then, in his words, he takes you by the hand — a firm grip — and with tears in his eyes asks, “Why will you die?” Don’t drift out of reach through sheer carelessness, he pleads. Don’t turn away from the one who loves you. And if you do, he says, at least admit that he did his best for you: “God knoweth I wrote each line for your eternal good.”

But he also speaks to the reader who has trusted Jesus. Stay with this. Let free grace be the way you live, not just the way you started. Living from a free gift does something unusual to a person: “To receive all as a free gift preserves the mind from self-righteous pride, and from self-accusing despair.” It makes you warm and grateful instead of anxious and driven. People trying to save themselves by doing their best, he says, never know that kind of joy. A slave can obey out of fear; a child loved by his father obeys out of something better. Years of going through religious motions, Spurgeon warns, can mean nothing to God, while “a glance from the eye of true faith is spiritual and it is therefore dear to Him.” Start with the inside, and the outside will follow.

And then: tell others. Your own soul won’t stay healthy unless you care about other people finding what you found. “The life of your soul lies in faith; its health lies in love.” He puts it even more sharply: anyone who has no longing to lead others to Jesus “has never been under the spell of love himself.” Start at home. Then your neighbours. Then your street. Spread the message wherever your hand can reach.

His last words are an urgent plea not to put it off. “You have had enough of resolving, come to action.” Trust Jesus now, decisively, today. It may be now or never. “Let it be NOW; it would be horrible that it should be never.” And the book’s final line is a farewell and an invitation in one: “meet me in heaven.”

Now — what is this actually about? Grace isn’t something to think about forever; it’s something to receive and then live from. It’s possible to read a whole book about grace, agree with every page, and still never actually trust Jesus — like standing in a food shop and walking out hungry. “Someday” feels safe, but Spurgeon is honest that you don’t own someday. Today is the only day you’ve definitely got.

And if you have received it, the rest of your life is meant to be shaped by it. Not proud, because none of it was earned. Not crushed, because none of it can be lost by your failure. Grateful. Warm. Busy with love for the people around you. That’s what a life that is “all of grace” looks like from the outside. It started with a knock at the door in chapter one. The only question left is whether you’ll open it — and Spurgeon would say: why not today?

One thing to do this week: decide. If you’ve never actually trusted Jesus, don’t make another resolution about doing it later — tell him today, in your own words, that you are taking the free gift and leaning your whole weight on him. If you already trust him, think of one person you care about and, this week, tell them in a sentence or two what grace has meant to you.

study_questions.question: What does Spurgeon say he did when he reached this last page of the book?
study_questions.answer: He put down his pen and knelt to pray for everyone who would read it, and then pictured himself taking the reader by the hand and pleading with them not to turn away from Jesus.

study_questions.question: How does receiving everything as a free gift protect a person from both pride and despair?
study_questions.answer: Since nothing was earned, there is nothing to be proud of; and since it rests on God’s grace rather than our performance, our failures can’t make us hopeless. It produces grateful love instead.

study_questions.question: Is there something you’ve kept “resolving” to do about God but haven’t done? What would it look like to act today?
study_questions.answer: The chapter’s point: book-reading is worthless unless the truth is taken hold of. Grace is to be received now — “Let it be NOW” — and then lived out in love for others.
